Olá is the neutral A1 greeting. In Brazil, você is the default way to address both strangers and acquaintances, and the verb takes the third-person form: você fala.

You make a short upbeat comment about where you are.

Ajuda is the neutral A1 word for help at a counter, a station, or a pharmacy. Socorro sounds more urgent, like an emergency, so this lesson sticks with a calm request.

Inside a bright cafe, a short upbeat comment.
Confirm a plan for tomorrow at seven.
You wrap up the scene with thanks and a goodbye.
A short confirmation of a plan with a time anchor and a friendly yes.
As you wrap up, you casually confirm the plan for tomorrow at seven.
Amanhã is the A1 time anchor for simple planning. The grave accent on às marks the contraction of a + as for clock times; without the accent, as is just the plural article.
Late afternoon, a quick confirmation of tomorrow’s plan.
Close the scene with thanks and a casual Brazilian goodbye.
A simple closer with thanks and the casual goodbye that Brazilians use all the time.
On your way out, you give a quick thanks and a casual goodbye.
In Portuguese, obrigado/obrigada is marked by the speaker, not the listener: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada. The exercise accepts both, even though the canonical display uses obrigado.
The exit of a cafe, a quick thank-you and a casual goodbye.

At the shop counter, you openly say you don't understand and you need a hand.
Entendo is the A1 "I" form of entender. Portuguese negates simply with não placed before the verb — no double negative needed.
Bright counter, a short pause, a calm request for help.

Could you write that down, please?
At the counter, you ask someone to write down a number or address.
Escrever is the A1 verb for getting things in writing. With você, the modal pode stays in the third-person singular form — same shape you would use with ele or ela.
A notepad on the counter as an exact detail is written down.
Ask someone to show a place on a map or phone.

A request to point out a place visibly on a map or phone screen.
Can you show me on the map?
On the sidewalk, you hold out your phone and ask for a visible pointer.
Mapa is masculine in Portuguese — o mapa, despite ending in -a. No mapa is the standard contraction of em + o, a pattern you will use constantly.
A phone map between two people, a finger tracing the route.

At the bakery, you compare two visible options on the counter.

Two visible pastries, a quick choice question.

A quick question to check whether an item is currently in stock.

At the till, you quickly ask whether you can pay by card.
Cartão ends in the classic Portuguese nasal -ão, pronounced through the nose. Keep the tilde when you can, but the app accepts cartao without it.
A card reader at a bright till, a quick payment question.

The receipt and a bag, please.
A short closing request after paying.
The receipt and a bag, please.
After paying, you ask for the receipt and a bag.
Sacola is the everyday Brazilian word for a shop bag — in Portugal you would more often hear saco. The feminine uma signals its gender: a sacola.
A till, a receipt, and a small shopping bag.

You do a quick check that this is the right option.

Reserva is feminine, so it takes uma. Em nome de is the standard Brazilian phrase for naming who the booking is under — you will hear it at restaurants, hotels, and clinics.
A reservation list at the host stand, a calm arrival.
Before choosing, boarding, or buying, confirm that this is the correct one.
A quick confirmation before you commit to an item or a place.
Before getting on or buying, you do a quick check that this is the right one.
Certo is the most natural Brazilian tag for right? It works at a bus stop, a ticket window, or a shop counter — anywhere you want a quick yes-or-no check.
A pointing gesture before a decision, a quick confirmation.
At a counter or in a social moment, ask for a brief pause.
A short request for time while you look for a card, a word, or an answer.
At the till, you need a moment and calmly ask for one.
Um momento, por favor is the go-to A1 phrase for buying yourself a few seconds. Momento is masculine, which is why it takes um (not uma).
A brief pause at the counter while looking for a card or a word.

You reply warmly after an introduction.
A neutral first-meeting question for someone’s name.
First meeting — you ask for the other person's name neutrally.

Politely postpone a plan to the next day.

You can't fully commit and softly push the plan to tomorrow.

Close a casual meeting with a see-you-tomorrow goodbye.
